title: Micropipette Aspiration of Substrate-attached Cells to Estimate Cell Stiffness
protocol: Pull glass micropipettes using a micropipette puller or microforge.
Select borosilicate glass capillaries with an external diameter of approximately 1.5 mm and an internal diameter of approximately 1.4 mm.
Pull a glass capillary in the middle until it starts to melt.
Separate the two halves of the melted capillary to generate micropipettes.
Optimize the parameters on a commercial puller for desired pipette shape and size.
Verify under microscope that pipette tips approximate cylindrical tubes.
Adjust heat and pull settings to achieve tip diameters between 2 to 6 μm external diameter.
Ensure optimal length of pipette shank based on expected deformation.
Fire-polish the tip of the pipette using a microforge.
Fill the micropipette with physiological saline solution, such as PBS or non-fluorescent growth media.
Supplement the solution in the micropipette with 30% serum.
Immerse the tip of the pipette into the solution to allow liquid to fill by capillary forces.
Backfill the pipette from the other end to eliminate air bubbles.
Alternatively, fill the whole pipette from the back end and gently tap on the shank to remove bubbles.
Warm PBS solution.
Dilute the stock diI to a working concentration (5 μM) with the warmed PBS solution.
Sonicate for 5 min to break dye aggregates.
Spin down for 5 min and take supernatant.
Wash cells in PBS 3 times, 5 min each.
Incubate cells with the dye solution for 30 min in a 37 °C incubator.
Wash the cells with PBS 3 times for 5 min each.
Mount the cells into a microaspiration chamber on an inverted fluorescent microscope.
Position the cells, choosing one for an experiment and placing it in the center of the visual field.
Place a micropipette filled with PBS/media w/ serum solution into a pipette holder connected to a power transducer by flexible tubing.
Equilibrate the pressure in the pipette to atmospheric pressure at the beginning of each experiment.
Position the micropipette at a shallow angle to the bottom of the chamber and bring its tip to the center of the visual field.
Position the pipette at the shallowest angle possible (10-15°) and flex the shank against the bottom of the chamber.
Slowly bring down the micropipette to the side of a single cell using the course manipulator until near the plane of focus for the cell.
Move the micropipette to the edge of the cell until the tip gently touches the membrane.
Take one image to observe the position of the pipette.
Apply a step of negative pressure using the transducer and maintain it until membrane projection is stabilized.
When the pressure is applied, gradually deform the membrane into the pipette until stabilized.
Acquire images every 30 seconds to track membrane deformation progression into the pipette.
Increase pressure to the next level in increments of 2-5 mm Hg.
Repeat the entire procedure until membrane projection detaches from the cell and moves into the pipette.
Stop the experiment once the membrane projection is inside the pipette.
Measure the aspirated length (L) from the tip of the pipette to the vertex of the circumference of the membrane projection.
Normalize the aspirated length for the pipette diameter (D) measured in each experiment.
